chapter_theme: A song at Kandanur (கந்தனூர்): after births in every form, the poet cries 'give me the state of jnana now' and asks whether Murugan will not come as father and mother run to embrace a leaping child; the praise names the vel against the fire-eyed demons and Siva with the Mother as his half.

897.reading: The poet speaks of the forms divided from bindu, moving and unmoving lives in every direction, through which he has come and wandered, and of the body that falls away; when he, lower than a dog, cries in pain 'come and give me the state of jnana this instant', he asks whether Murugan will not think of him as a father and mother melt and embrace the child who leaps toward them. The praise names the vel that destroyed the fire-eyed ones who come roaring like thunder in the dark, so the gods returned to Indra's world, and Murugan the son of Siva with the moon in his hair, who helps the poet's life, with the Mother in his half who stands everywhere, at Kandanur.
897.nuance: மைந்தர் தாவிப் புகழ தந்தை தாய் உற்றுருகி வந்து சேயைத் தழுவல்: grace pictured as parents running to the child who leaps toward them, a tender image rare in the book. விந்து பேதித்த வடிவங்கள்: births as forms differentiated from bindu. The first quatrain's syntax (மிஞ்ச நீ விட்ட வடிவங்களாலே) is uncertain, and the fire-eyed ones may be asuras or Death's servants.

links.note: 897 asks whether Murugan will not, as father and mother melt and embrace the child who leaps toward them (தந்தை தாய் உற்றுருகி வந்து சேயைத் தழுவல்), come to him crying for jnana. Tirumanthiram 2627 says the poet called his Lord as a calf calls, and the Lord sought him out and entered his body (நாடிவந்து உள்புகுந்தானே). Both picture grace as the parent who comes running to the child's cry; the Tirumanthiram reports it as done, the song asks for it.
